correctness.rationale: The proof separates domination from matching. Necessity of \(b_1\ge1\) and \(a_p\ge1\) follows from the endpoint twin classes together with perfect matchability. The cumulative inequalities are necessary because selected vertices in \(A_1\cup\cdots\cup A_k\) can only be matched into \(B_1\cup\cdots\cup B_k\). They are sufficient by Hall's theorem because for nonempty \(X\subseteq S_A\), taking the largest class index \(k\) met by \(X\) gives \(|X|\le\sum_{i\le k}a_i\le\sum_{i\le k}b_i=|N(X)|\). Equal selected side sizes then give a perfect matching. Exhaustive replay over 510 profiles of order at most 10 agrees on 348500 subsets and on the polynomial recurrence.

value.rationale: The paired-domination polynomial records every backup-compatible dominating placement by size, which is strictly richer than the minimum and upper parameters. For chain graphs, the theorem compresses simultaneous domination and perfect-matching feasibility to a natural one-dimensional ballot condition on canonical twin classes. This gives an exact enumerator, a direct dynamic program, and the exact multiplicity \(\alpha_p\beta_1\) of minimum solutions. The result is structural rather than an arbitrary finite slice or a known-table recomputation.
